strengths: The paper introduces a useful task combining reference images and modification text to retrieve the same person. ITCPR provides a potentially valuable evaluation resource with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b09/review-experiment-s8rfkdwo/call-cd1f4a3f00c4409da500d694d57eabc2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The two-stage framework is coherent and practical: person-specific CLIP fine-tuning followed by a lightweight image-to-token mapper uses existing image-caption and identity supervision without requiring composed-query training triplets.

The gains over simple fusion with the same fine-tuned encoders are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Rank-1 improves from 32.016% to 45.549%, and mAP from 41.831% to 55.260% (Table 1), supporting the usefulness of learned composition.

The paper includes informative ablations of supervision, data volume, filtering, mapper architecture, and fusion. Table 2 supports the benefits of text supervision and identity-aware matching. Clear pipeline diagrams, optimization settings, and supplementary timing results aid understanding and reproduction.
weaknesses: The headline comparison with Pic2Word is confounded. Table 1 explicitly states that Pic2Word's mapper was trained with the original CLIP parameters, even when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders; Word4Per's mapper is trained for those encoders. This representation mismatch prevents attributing the reported margin to the proposed method. Table 2 provides a useful partial control, but matched retraining of Pic2Word and evaluation of the closely related textual-inversion method cited as [2] are missing.

Methodological originality is limited and insufficiently distinguished from prior work. Image-to-pseudo-word mapping followed by text composition already underlies Pic2Word and related approaches. The main changes combine established person-retrieval fine-tuning and matching losses with textual supervision. The new benchmark is the clearest original contribution, making its validation particularly important.

The model-selection protocol is unclear. ITCPR is designated exclusively for testing, yet the supplementary experiments select optimal mapper architectures and fusion configurations using its reported performance. No independent validation procedure is specified, creating a risk of optimistic evaluation. Missing repeated runs or uncertainty estimates also weaken conclusions about smaller architectural and ensemble gains.

Benchmark documentation and validation are incomplete. The paper does not report annotator counts, agreement measurements, or the retrieval depth used when auditing additional positives. Aggregate results lack breakdowns by source dataset or modification type, limiting assessment of robustness across the heterogeneous sources and beyond the illustrated clothing changes.

Ethical reporting is inadequate for the stated surveillance application and planned dataset release. The paper should document permissions and applicable restrictions for repurposing identifiable person images, and address privacy, misuse, and demographic performance concerns associated with tracking people across clothing changes.
